title: The Body in Grief
hook: Grief folds the body inward around what it has lost, and the most useful thing another body can do is stay near it.
why:
Everyone grieves, and almost everyone is unsure what to do when someone else is grieving. Men in particular are often given few words and fewer models: stand at the graveside, shake hands, say *sorry for your loss*, and then go back to normal. Meanwhile the grieving man's body tells a long story that most people around him do not know how to read, and some read badly, deciding that he is not grieving enough, or too much, or in the wrong way.

This chapter is about reading grief and staying with it. You will learn what grief does to the body, why grieving people move back and forth between sorrow and ordinary life, how grief can strain the heart in the most literal sense, why people grieve in different styles, what helps and what does not, how grief comes in waves long after others have moved on, and when grief that has become stuck needs more than friends can give. The chapter on the quiet body in Part VI said the end of all this skill is a presence other people can rest in. Nowhere does that matter more than here.

teach.p:
Grief is not only a feeling. It is a full-body state, and much of it is visible. Crying, of course, and the breath patterns of crying described in the chapter on breath, but also frequent sighing, a heavy tiredness, slowed movement and a body that seems to curl around itself: shoulders rounded, head bowed, arms wrapped around the chest or the knees, the face in the hands. The grief plates in the pose library show some of these shapes.

Grief also disrupts the body's routines. Sleep breaks up. Appetite disappears or turns to comfort eating. Concentration fails, and grieving people often describe a fog: losing keys, forgetting appointments, reading the same paragraph again and again. Some feel physical pain, a heaviness in the chest, a tightness in the throat. Some become restless, unable to sit, walking for hours. Some look for the person who has died, turning at a familiar voice in a crowd, expecting them to come through the door.

None of this is a sign that something is wrong with the grieving person. It is what bodies do after a loss, and it can last much longer than people around the bereaved expect: months, and in waves for years.

For a reader, the lesson is to expect grief to show, and to show differently in different people. Some will be visibly undone. Some will look almost unchanged in public and collapse in private. The grief plates are not a checklist. They are a reminder that the body carries loss, and that what you see is only part of what is there.

Do not measure someone's grief by how much of it you can see.
teach.disconfirm: If bereaved people showed no more disruption of sleep, appetite, concentration and movement than anyone else, grief would be a feeling without a body. The experience of almost everyone who has grieved, and the research described below, suggest otherwise.
teach.pullQuote: Do not measure someone's grief by how much of it you can see.

teach.p:
People often imagine grief as a steady state that slowly fades, or as a series of stages to be passed through in order. In 1999 Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut proposed a different picture, which they called the dual process model. Grieving people, they argued, move back and forth between two kinds of activity. In loss-oriented moments they face the loss directly: crying, remembering, looking at photographs, yearning. In restoration-oriented moments they turn to the business of living: sorting out the house, going back to work, learning new tasks, taking a break from grief by watching a film or seeing friends. Both are part of healthy grieving, and the movement between them is the point.

This explains something that often confuses observers. A widower laughing at the wake, a son joking with his brothers the day after their father's death, a mother going back to work a week after a funeral: none of them is failing to grieve. They are in a restoration moment, and the loss will come back.

Research by George Bonanno and colleagues has added a further surprise: many bereaved people show considerable resilience, functioning reasonably well within months, without this meaning they loved the person less. In one study of bereaved spouses, Dacher Keltner and Bonanno found that genuine laughter while talking about the person who had died went with less distress, not more, and with warmer responses from others.

So read grief over time, not in a single moment. A grieving man who is smiling today may be in pieces tomorrow, and both are real.
teach.disconfirm: If grieving people who laughed, worked and took breaks from sorrow early on later fared worse than those who grieved continuously, the dual process view would be wrong. The research described here found the opposite, though every person's path is different.

teach.p:
The phrase *a broken heart* is more than a metaphor. In 2012 Elizabeth Mostofsky and colleagues studied nearly two thousand people who had had a heart attack and compared the timing of the attack with recent losses in their lives. In the twenty-four hours after the death of someone significant to them, the rate of heart attacks was about twenty-one times higher than usual. The risk fell steadily over the following days and weeks.

The numbers behind that estimate are small, and the absolute risk for any one bereaved person remains low. But the finding fits what is known about grief as a stress state: a racing heart, raised blood pressure, broken sleep, missed meals and forgotten medication, all at once, in people who may already have heart disease. Doctors also recognise a rarer condition, sometimes called broken heart syndrome, in which sudden severe emotional stress temporarily weakens the heart muscle.

For a reader, this has practical consequences. In the days after a death, look out for the bereaved, especially older people and those with heart conditions. Make sure they are eating, sleeping where possible and taking their usual medication. Do not dismiss chest pain, breathlessness or fainting as grief; call for medical help.

It also makes sense of something many bereaved people describe: a physical ache in the chest. It is real, and it is worth taking seriously.

In the first days after a loss, care for the body as well as the heart.
teach.disconfirm: If heart attacks were no more common in the days after a significant death than at other times, the physical warning in this block would be unnecessary. The study found a sharp rise, though based on a small number of cases, so it is a reason for care rather than alarm.

teach.p:
Kenneth Doka and Terry Martin, in *Grieving Beyond Gender*, describe a continuum of grieving styles. At one end is intuitive grieving, in which grief is felt and expressed mainly through emotion: crying, talking about feelings, seeking comfort from others. At the other is instrumental grieving, in which grief is experienced more through thought and expressed mainly through activity: doing things, solving problems, building, organising, remembering the person by acting for them. Most people blend the two.

Doka and Martin originally linked these styles to gender, and many men do lean towards the instrumental end, but they later stressed that gender is only one influence among many, and that plenty of women grieve instrumentally and plenty of men intuitively.

Instrumental grief is often misread. A man who rarely cries, goes back to work quickly, throws himself into sorting out the estate or rebuilding the garden, or organises a charity run in his late wife's name, may be judged by others as cold or as avoiding his grief. He may be grieving deeply, in the way that is most natural to him. Pressing him to talk about his feelings may feel like being asked to grieve in a foreign language.

The practical lesson is to meet people in their style. For an intuitive griever, sitting and talking may be the help. For an instrumental griever, working alongside him, side by side, on a task connected to the person who died, may let him talk in a way that a conversation across a table never would.

Grief that looks like doing is still grief.
teach.disconfirm: If people who grieved mainly through activity fared consistently worse than those who grieved mainly through talking and tears, instrumental grief would be avoidance rather than a style. Doka and Martin's work suggests the styles are different paths, not better and worse ones.

teach.h: What helps, and what does not.
teach.p:
The most useful thing you can offer a grieving person is presence. Turn up. Sit with them. Say the name of the person who died, because many bereaved people say that what hurts most is everyone else avoiding it. Ask about them: *Tell me about him.* Let silences happen.

Practical help often matters more than words. Meals, lifts, help with forms and phone calls, mowing the lawn, picking up children, sorting the post. Offer specific things rather than *let me know if you need anything*, which puts the burden of asking on the person least able to bear it. *I'm bringing dinner on Thursday. Is six all right?* is easier to accept.

Some well-meant phrases tend to hurt. *At least he had a long life*, *everything happens for a reason*, *she's in a better place*, *I know how you feel*, *you need to be strong for the children*: each tries to shrink or explain the loss, and many bereaved people describe them as the hardest things they heard. A simple *I'm so sorry* and your continued presence say more.

Touch may help, or it may not. The chapter on touch said to ask, and grief does not change that. An open hand, an arm offered, sitting close enough that they can lean on you if they want to, leave the choice with them.

And do not disappear. Most support arrives in the first fortnight and fades after the funeral. The months after, when the casseroles stop and everyone else has moved on, are often the hardest. Put the anniversary in your calendar.
teach.disconfirm: If bereaved people reported that platitudes such as at least he had a long life helped as much as presence, practical help and hearing the name of the person who died, this block's advice would not matter. Bereaved people's accounts consistently suggest otherwise.

teach.p:
Long after the funeral, grief keeps coming back, often suddenly. A song in a shop, a smell, a date, a place, a photograph found in a drawer, the first Christmas, the birthday, the anniversary: any of these can bring a wave of grief as strong as the first days, months or even years later. Bereaved people often describe being ambushed by it.

The body shows the wave. A man in a supermarket may suddenly go still, his breath catching, and walk out leaving his trolley. A colleague may leave a meeting abruptly and come back ten minutes later with red eyes. A friend at a wedding may go quiet during the father-and-daughter dance. To an observer who does not know the history, these moments can look like rudeness, illness or moodiness.

For a reader, two things follow. First, keep a longer memory of other people's losses than they might expect you to. Note the anniversary of a friend's bereavement. Be gentle around birthdays, holidays and the dates you know about. A message on the first anniversary, *thinking of you and of her today*, often means more than anything said at the funeral.

Second, when someone suddenly withdraws, goes quiet or leaves, put grief on your list of rivals, especially if you know of a loss. Do not demand an explanation. A quiet *you all right?* later, or simply making space, is enough.

A wave is not a relapse. It is grief doing what grief does.
teach.disconfirm: If grief, once it had eased, did not return in waves around anniversaries and reminders, the advice to remember dates would matter less. Most bereaved people describe exactly these waves, often years later.

teach.p:
For most people, grief changes over time. It does not disappear, but it becomes something they can carry alongside their lives. For a minority, it does not: months later, the yearning is as intense as at the start, the person cannot accept the death, life has lost all meaning, and they cannot function at work or at home. Psychiatry now recognises this as prolonged grief disorder. The World Health Organization's classification looks for it at least six months after a death, and the American system at least twelve months.

You are not in a position to diagnose it, and should not try. What you can notice is a pattern that has not shifted at all after many months: a person who has stopped functioning, stopped eating properly, cut themselves off from everyone, is drinking heavily, or speaks of wanting to be with the person who died.

When you see that pattern, encourage the person to talk to their doctor. Specialist bereavement support and therapies for prolonged grief exist and help. Many areas have bereavement services that people can contact directly. Offer practical help in getting there.

And if a grieving person says they want to join the person who died, or that they cannot go on without them, take it seriously. Ask them directly whether they are thinking of ending their life. Grief is a time of raised risk, and asking does not put the idea in their head. The chapter on suicidal ideation explains how to respond, and the crisis resources are one tap from the home screen.

Most grief needs company. Some grief needs more, and part of staying near is noticing when.
teach.disconfirm: If grief that remained intense and disabling many months after a loss eased just as well without specialist help as with it, encouraging professional support would add little. The recognition of prolonged grief disorder reflects evidence that some people need, and benefit from, more.

poseGallery.doCaption: 'I'm so sorry. Tell me about him.'
poseGallery.dontCaption: 'At least he had a long life.'
poseGallery.annotation: Platitudes try to shrink the loss. Presence, and hearing the name of the person who died, help far more.

poseGallery.doCaption: Knowing grief comes and goes, and some people grieve by doing.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Deciding he can't have cared, since he's back at work and joking.
poseGallery.annotation: Grieving people move between sorrow and ordinary life, and instrumental grievers express grief through action. Neither means less love.

poseGallery.doCaption: Turning up in month three with a meal, and on the anniversary.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Disappearing once the funeral is over.
poseGallery.annotation: Support fades after the first fortnight, when the hardest months begin. Remembering later often means the most.

poseGallery.doCaption: Sitting close, and leaving the choice of touch to him.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Hugging him because he looks like he needs it.
poseGallery.annotation: Grief does not change the rule on touch. Offer, sit close enough to lean on, and let the grieving person choose.

caseStudy:
Andy, forty, and his sister Claire lose their mother in February. Their father, Bill, sixty-seven, has been married to her for forty-four years. At the funeral he shakes every hand and does not cry. A week later he is back at his allotment, and then he starts rebuilding the shed she always complained about. Claire tells Andy, upset, that Dad does not seem to care.

Andy is not so sure. He has noticed that Bill's walk has slowed, that he sighs often, that he has stopped eating breakfast, and that he works on the shed from first light until dark. He has also noticed that Bill always takes his heart pills with breakfast, and wonders whether he is taking them now. He asks. Bill admits he has forgotten them most days. Andy puts them by the kettle with a note.

Andy does not ask his father how he is feeling. He turns up on Saturdays with his tools, and they work on the shed together, side by side. On the third Saturday, measuring a window frame, Bill says that Mum wanted a window just here so she could watch the birds, and that he is building it the way she wanted. Then he talks about her for an hour while they work, more than he has talked about anything in years.

Andy explains to Claire what he has seen: that Dad is grieving by building, and that it is real. Claire starts bringing lunch on Saturdays.

On the anniversary in February, Andy rings in the morning. Bill's voice catches on the first word, and he says he is fine, and then that he is not, and then that he is glad Andy rang. In the spring they put a bird feeder outside the new window.
observe: Think of someone you know who has been bereaved in the past year, and notice whether they seem to grieve more by feeling or by doing.
Notice the phrases people use to comfort the bereaved, and which ones try to shrink or explain the loss.
Look through your calendar and note any anniversaries of losses among people close to you.

drills.name: Name and Calendar
steps: List the people close to you who have lost someone in the past two years.
For each, note the name of the person who died, if you know it.
Find out, if you can, the date of the death or the funeral.
Put a reminder in your calendar a day before each anniversary.
On the day, send a short message that mentions the person by name.

drills.name: Specific Offers
steps: Write down three things you have said, or heard said, to bereaved people that put the burden of asking on them, such as let me know if you need anything.
For each, write a specific offer instead, with a day and time.
Write three phrases you will avoid and what you will say instead.
Say the specific offers aloud.
Use one of them the next time someone you know is bereaved.

drills.name: Style Check
steps: Think back to a loss in your own life.
Write down what you did in the weeks after it: what you felt, what you said, what you did with your hands and your time.
Mark whether your grief leaned towards feeling or towards doing.
Note how other people responded to your way of grieving.
Write what would have helped most, given your style.

drills.name: Side-by-Side Support
steps: Think of someone grieving who seems to grieve by doing rather than talking.
Identify a task connected to their loss, or simply a practical task they need done.
Offer to help with it, alongside them.
While you work, follow their lead in conversation; do not steer it towards feelings.
Afterwards, note anything they said about the person who died.

drills.name: Know the Thresholds
steps: Write down the signs in this chapter that grief may have become stuck.
Write down the signs that a grieving person may be at risk, including talk of wanting to join the person who died.
Find bereavement support services available where you live and note how to contact them.
Find the crisis resources in this app for your region.
Keep these notes where you can find them.

quiz.q: Three weeks after his wife's funeral, a colleague is back at work, busy and even joking. What does this chapter suggest?
options: That he cannot have been very close to her, given how quickly he has recovered
That he is in denial and should be encouraged to talk about his feelings
That grief comes and goes, and some people grieve by doing; keep checking in
That he is fully over the loss and no longer needs any support at all
quiz.explain: Grieving people move between facing the loss and attending to life, and instrumental grievers express grief through action. Neither means less love. Keep remembering, especially in the months ahead and on the anniversary.

quiz.q: What does Stroebe and Schut's dual process model of grief propose?
options: Bereaved people move back and forth between facing the loss and attending to life
Bereaved people pass through five fixed stages of grief in a set order
Bereaved people who take breaks from grieving are avoiding their loss
Bereaved people should face the loss continuously until the grief has gone
quiz.explain: Both loss-oriented moments, such as crying and remembering, and restoration-oriented ones, such as work and distraction, are part of healthy grieving. The movement between them is the point.

quiz.q: What did Mostofsky and colleagues find in the twenty-four hours after the death of someone significant?
options: Heart attacks became less common, as people rested more after a death
There was no change at all in the rate of heart attacks after a death
Heart attacks became more common only among people under forty years old
The rate of heart attacks was about twenty-one times higher than usual
quiz.explain: The rate was sharply raised in the first day and fell steadily afterwards. The numbers were small and the absolute risk remains low, but it is a reason to look after the bereaved physically, especially those with heart conditions.

quiz.q: A friend's father has just died. What is most likely to help in the first weeks?
options: Telling him that at least his father lived a long and full life
Turning up, offering specific help, and saying his father's name
Waiting until he gets in touch, so that you do not intrude on him
Reminding him that he needs to be strong for the rest of the family
quiz.explain: Presence, practical help offered with a day and time, and hearing the name of the person who died help most. Platitudes and waiting to be asked tend to leave grieving people more alone.

quiz.q: What do Doka and Martin call grief that is experienced and expressed mainly through thought and activity rather than open emotion?
options: Delayed grief
Absent grief
Instrumental grieving
Complicated or prolonged grief
quiz.explain: Instrumental grievers often express grief by doing, building or organising, and are often misread as not grieving. It is a style, not a failure, and meeting them side by side, in action, often helps them talk.

quiz.q: Eight months after her husband died, your aunt barely leaves the house, has stopped eating properly, and says she just wants to be with him. What fits this chapter?
options: Ask her directly if she is thinking of ending her life, and help her reach help
Reassure her that time heals everything and that she will feel better soon
Leave her be, since grief is private and must simply be waited out
Tell her she is grieving the wrong way and needs to move on with her life
quiz.explain: Wanting to be with the person who died is a reason to ask directly about suicide, which does not plant the idea. Combined with months of withdrawal and not eating, it also suggests she needs more than company, so help her reach her doctor or a crisis line.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific loss in your own life, or in the life of someone close to you. Describe what grief did to the body: sleep, appetite, movement, breath, concentration. Did the grief lean more towards feeling or towards doing? What did other people say or do that helped, and what hurt? Then think of someone you know who is grieving now or will be soon. What specific thing could you do in the months after the funeral, when most support fades?
reflection.guidance: Many men find that their own grief was misread, or that they misread someone else's, because it looked like doing rather than feeling. Try to describe the body before the emotion. The last question should produce something concrete, with a date if possible: a meal, a visit, a message on an anniversary.

failureMode: The commonest failure is to judge grief by how it looks, deciding that someone who is working, joking or dry-eyed cannot really be grieving, or that someone still weeping months later is grieving wrong. The second is to reach for platitudes that shrink the loss. The third is to offer vague help, *let me know if you need anything*, and then to disappear after the funeral, just as the hardest months begin. The fourth is to miss the body: the forgotten medication, the chest pain dismissed as grief, the meals not eaten. And the most serious is to hear a grieving person say they want to join the one they lost and to let it pass. Stay near, offer specific help, remember the dates, and when grief is stuck or someone is at risk, help them reach more.
